title: V. The Third Ordeal
paragraphs: Though Mitya spoke sullenly, it was evident that he was now trying harder than ever not to forget or skip a single detail of his story. He told them how he had leapt over the fence into his father’s garden; how he had gone up to the window; told them everything that had happened under the window. Clearly, precisely, distinctly, he described the feelings that troubled him during those moments in the garden, when he longed so desperately to know whether Grushenka was with his father or not. But, strange to say, both the lawyers now listened with a kind of dreadful reserve, looked at him coldly, asked few questions. Mitya could read nothing from their faces.
“They’re angry and offended,” he thought. “Well, to hell with them!”

When he described how he had finally made up his mind to give the “signal” to his father that Grushenka had come, so that he would open the window, the lawyers paid no attention to the word “signal,” as though they entirely failed to grasp the meaning of the word in this context — so much so that Mitya noticed it. Coming at last to the moment when, on seeing his father peering out of the window, his hatred flared up and he pulled the pestle out of his pocket, he suddenly, as though on purpose, stopped short. He sat staring at the wall and was aware that their eyes were fixed on him.
“Well?” said the investigating lawyer. “You pulled out the weapon and ... and what happened then?”
“Then? Why, then I murdered him ... hit him on the head and cracked his skull.... I suppose that’s your version. That’s it!”
His eyes suddenly flashed. All his smothered anger suddenly flared up with extraordinary violence in his soul.
“Our version?” repeated Nikolay Parfenovitch. “Well — and yours?”
Mitya dropped his eyes and was silent for a long time.

“My version, gentlemen? Well, it was like this,” he began softly. “Whether it was somebody’s tears, or my mother praying to God, or a good angel kissing me at that instant, I don’t know. But the devil was defeated. I tore away from the window and ran to the fence. My father was startled and for the first time saw me then, cried out, and sprang back from the window. I remember that very well. I ran across the garden to the fence ... and there Grigory caught me, when I was sitting on the fence.”
At that point he at last raised his eyes and looked at his listeners. They seemed to be staring at him with perfectly unruffled attention. A sort of spasm of indignation seized Mitya’s soul.
“Why, you’re laughing at me at this very moment, gentlemen!” he broke off suddenly.
“What makes you think that?” observed Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“You don’t believe a word — that’s why! I understand, of course, that I have come to the crucial point. The old man is lying there now with his skull broken, while I — after dramatically describing how I wanted to kill him, and how I grabbed the pestle — suddenly run away from the window. A romance! Poetry! As if anyone could take a man at his word. Ha ha! You are scoffers, gentlemen!”
And he spun around on his chair so hard that it creaked.
“And did you notice,” the prosecutor asked suddenly, as if ignoring Mitya’s excitement, “did you notice, when you ran away from the window, whether the door into the garden was open?”
“No, it was not open.”
“It was not?”
“It was shut. And who could have opened it? Bah! the door. Wait a bit!” he seemed suddenly to catch himself, and almost with a start:
“Why, did you find the door open?”
“Yes, it was open.”
“Why, who could have opened it, if you didn’t open it yourselves?” cried Mitya, greatly astonished.

“The door stood open, and your father’s murderer undoubtedly went in through that door, and, having committed the crime, went out again by the same door,” the prosecutor pronounced deliberately, as though chiseling out each word separately. “That is perfectly clear. The murder was committed in the room and not through the window; that is absolutely certain from the investigation that has been made, from the position of the body and everything else. There can be no doubt about that fact.”
Mitya was absolutely dumbfounded.

“But that is utterly impossible!” he cried, completely at a loss. “I ... I didn’t go in.... I tell you positively, definitely, the door was shut the whole time I was in the garden, and when I ran out of the garden. I only stood at the window and saw him through the window. That’s all, that’s all.... I remember everything to the last minute. And even if I didn’t remember, it would still be the same. I know it, because no one knew the signals except Smerdyakov, and me, and the dead man. And he wouldn’t have opened the door to anyone in the world without the signals.”

“Signals? What signals?” asked the prosecutor, with greedy, almost hysterical curiosity. Instantly he lost all trace of his reserve and dignity. He put the question with a kind of cringing timidity. He had caught the scent of an important fact of which he had known nothing, and was already filled with dread that Mitya might be unwilling to disclose it.

“So you didn’t know!” Mitya winked at him with a malicious, mocking smile. “What if I won’t tell you? From whom could you find out? No one knew about the signals except my father, Smerdyakov, and me: that was all. Heaven knew too, but it won’t tell you. But it’s an interesting fact. There’s no telling what you could build on it. Ha ha! Take comfort, gentlemen, I’ll reveal it. You have some foolish idea in your heads. You don’t know the man you are dealing with! You are dealing with a prisoner who gives evidence against himself, to his own cost! Yes, for I am a man of honor, and you — are not.”

The prosecutor swallowed this without a murmur. He was trembling with impatience to hear the new fact. In minute detail, Mitya told them everything about the signals that Fyodor Pavlovitch had invented for Smerdyakov. He told them exactly what each tap on the window meant, tapped the signals out on the table, and when Nikolay Parfenovitch said that he assumed Mitya had tapped out the signal “Grushenka has come” when he tapped to his father, he answered precisely that he had tapped that signal, that “Grushenka had come.”
“So now you can build up your tower,” Mitya broke off, and again turned away from them contemptuously.
“So no one knew of the signals but your late father, you, and the servant Smerdyakov? And no one else?” Nikolay Parfenovitch inquired once more.
“Yes. The servant Smerdyakov, and Heaven. Write that down about Heaven. That may come in useful. Besides, you’ll need God yourselves.”
And of course they had already begun writing it down. But while they wrote, the prosecutor said suddenly, as though seizing on a new idea:

“But if Smerdyakov also knew of these signals, and you absolutely deny all responsibility for the death of your father, wasn’t it perhaps he who knocked out the agreed signal, got your father to open the door for him, and then ... committed the crime?”
Mitya turned on him a look of profound irony and intense hatred. His silent stare lasted so long that it made the prosecutor blink.

“You’ve caught the fox again,” Mitya commented at last; “you’ve got the beast by the tail. Ha ha! I see through you, Mr. Prosecutor. You assumed, of course, that I would jump at that, seize on your suggestion, and shout at the top of my voice, ‘Aha! it’s Smerdyakov; he’s the murderer.’ Admit it — that’s what you thought. Admit it, and I’ll go on.”
But the prosecutor did not admit it. He held his tongue and waited.
“You’re mistaken. I’m not going to shout ‘It’s Smerdyakov,’” said Mitya.
“And you don’t even suspect him?”
“Why, do you suspect him?”
“He is suspected, too.”
Mitya fixed his eyes on the floor.

“Joking aside,” he brought out gloomily. “Listen. From the very beginning, almost from the moment when I ran out from behind the curtain to you, the thought of Smerdyakov has been in my mind. I’ve been sitting here shouting that I’m innocent, and thinking the whole time ‘Smerdyakov!’ I can’t get Smerdyakov out of my head. In fact, I, too, thought of Smerdyakov just now; but only for a second. Almost at once I thought, ‘No, it’s not Smerdyakov.’ It’s not his doing, gentlemen.”
“In that case, is there anyone else you suspect?” Nikolay Parfenovitch inquired cautiously.
“I don’t know who it could be, whether it’s the hand of Heaven or of Satan, but ... not Smerdyakov,” Mitya jerked out decisively.
“But what makes you claim so confidently and so emphatically that it isn’t him?”

“From my conviction — my impression. Because Smerdyakov is a man of the most abject character and a coward. He’s not just a coward, he’s the epitome of all the cowardice in the world walking on two legs. He has the heart of a chicken. When he talked to me, he was always trembling with fear that I might kill him, though I never raised a hand against him. He fell at my feet and blubbered; he has literally kissed these very boots, begging me ‘not to frighten him.’ Do you hear? ‘Not to frighten him.’ What a thing to say! Why, I offered him money. He’s a whimpering chicken — sickly, epileptic, weak-minded — a child of eight could thrash him. He has no character worth speaking of. It’s not Smerdyakov, gentlemen. He doesn’t care for money; he wouldn’t take my presents. Besides, what motive did he have to murder the old man? Why, he’s very likely his son, you know — his natural son. Did you know that?”
“We have heard that legend. But you are your father’s son, too, aren’t you; yet you yourself told everyone you meant to murder him.”

“That’s a jab! And a nasty, mean one, too! I’m not afraid! Oh, gentlemen, isn’t it base of you to say that to my face? It’s base, because I told you that myself. I not only wanted to murder him, but I might have done it. And what’s more, I went out of my way to tell you of my own accord that I nearly murdered him. But you see, I didn’t murder him; you see, my guardian angel saved me — that’s what you haven’t taken into account. And that’s why it’s so base of you. Because I didn’t kill him, I didn’t kill him! Do you hear? I did not kill him.”
He was almost choking. He had not been so moved before during the entire interrogation.
“And what has he told you, gentlemen — Smerdyakov, I mean?” he added suddenly, after a pause. “May I ask that question?”

“You may ask any question,” the prosecutor replied with frigid severity, “any question relating to the facts of the case, and we, I repeat, are bound to answer every inquiry you make. We found the servant Smerdyakov, about whom you are asking, lying unconscious in his bed, in an epileptic fit of extreme severity, which had returned, perhaps, ten times. The doctor who was with us told us, after examining him, that he may not outlive the night.”
“Well, if that’s so, the devil must have killed him,” broke suddenly from Mitya, as though until that moment he had been asking himself: “Was it Smerdyakov or not?”
“We will come back to this later,” Nikolay Parfenovitch decided. “Now, wouldn’t you like to continue your statement?”

Mitya asked for a rest. His request was politely granted. After resting, he continued his story. But he was clearly depressed. He was exhausted, humiliated, and morally shaken. To make things worse, the prosecutor kept irritating him, as though on purpose, with vexatious interruptions about “trifling points.” Mitya had barely described how, sitting on the wall, he had struck Grigory on the head with the pestle while the old man had hold of his left leg, and how he had then jumped down to look at him, when the prosecutor stopped him to ask him to describe exactly how he had been sitting on the wall. Mitya was surprised.
“Oh, I was sitting like this, astride, one leg on one side of the wall and one on the other.”
“And the pestle?”
“The pestle was in my hand.”
“Not in your pocket? Do you remember that precisely? Was it a violent blow you gave him?”
“It must have been a violent one. But why do you ask?”
“Would you mind sitting on the chair just the way you were sitting on the wall then, and showing us just how you moved your arm, and in what direction?”
“You’re making fun of me, aren’t you?” asked Mitya, looking haughtily at the speaker; but the other man did not flinch.
Mitya turned abruptly, sat astride his chair, and swung his arm.
“This is how I struck him! That’s how I knocked him down! What more do you want?”
“Thank you. May I trouble you now to explain why you jumped down, with what purpose, and what you had in mind?”
“Oh, hang it!... I jumped down to look at the man I’d hurt ... I don’t know what for!”
“Though you were so excited and were running away?”
“Yes, though I was excited and running away.”
“You wanted to help him?”
“Help!... Yes, perhaps I did want to help him.... I don’t remember.”
“You don’t remember? Then you didn’t quite know what you were doing?”
“Not at all. I remember everything — every detail. I jumped down to look at him, and wiped his face with my handkerchief.”
“We have seen your handkerchief. Did you hope to restore him to consciousness?”
“I don’t know whether I hoped that. I just wanted to make sure whether he was alive or not.”
“Ah! You wanted to be sure? Well, what then?”
“I’m not a doctor. I couldn’t decide. I ran away thinking I’d killed him. And now he’s recovered.”
“Excellent,” commented the prosecutor. “Thank you. That’s all I wanted. Kindly proceed.”

Alas! it never entered Mitya’s head to tell them, though he remembered it, that he had jumped back out of pity, and that standing over the prostrate figure he had even uttered some words of regret: “You’ve come to grief, old man — there’s no help for it. Well, there you must lie.”

The prosecutor could only draw one conclusion: that the man had jumped back “at such a moment and in such a state of excitement, simply with the purpose of making sure whether the only witness of his crime was dead; that he must therefore have been a man of great strength, composure, resolve, and foresight, even at such a moment,” ... and so on. The prosecutor was satisfied: “I’ve provoked the high-strung fellow with ‘trifles’ and he has said more than he meant to.”
With painful effort Mitya went on. But this time he was pulled up immediately by Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“How did you come to run to the servant, Fedosya Markovna, with your hands so covered in blood, and, as it turns out, your face, too?”
“Why, I didn’t notice the blood at all at the time,” Mitya answered.
“That’s quite likely. It does happen sometimes.” The prosecutor exchanged glances with Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“I simply didn’t notice. You’re quite right there, prosecutor,” Mitya suddenly agreed.

Next came the account of Mitya’s sudden decision to “step aside” and make way for their happiness. But he could not bring himself to open his heart to them as he had before, and tell them about “the queen of his soul.” He disliked speaking of her in front of these chilly men, “who were fastening on him like bugs.” So in response to their repeated questions, he answered briefly and abruptly:

“Well, I made up my mind to kill myself. What had I left to live for? That question stared me in the face. Her first rightful lover had come back, the man who had wronged her, but who had hurried back to offer his love after five years and make amends for the wrong with marriage.... So I knew it was all over for me.... And behind me was disgrace, and that blood — Grigory’s.... What did I have to live for? So I went to redeem the pistols I had pawned, to load them and put a bullet in my brain tomorrow.”
“And a grand feast the night before?”

“Yes, a grand feast the night before. Damn it all, gentlemen! Do hurry up and finish it. I meant to shoot myself not far from here, beyond the village, and I’d planned to do it at five o’clock in the morning. And I already had a note in my pocket. I wrote it at Perhotin’s when I loaded my pistols. Here’s the letter. Read it! It’s not for your sake that I’m telling you,” he added contemptuously. He took it from his waistcoat pocket and flung it on the table. The lawyers read it with curiosity, and, as is customary, added it to the papers connected with the case.
“And you didn’t even think of washing your hands at Perhotin’s? You weren’t afraid of arousing suspicion?”

“What suspicion? Suspicion or not, I would have galloped here just the same, and shot myself at five o’clock, and you wouldn’t have been in time to do anything. If it hadn’t been for what happened to my father, you would have known nothing about it, and wouldn’t have come here. Oh, it’s the devil’s doing. It was the devil who murdered father, it was through the devil that you found out about it so soon. How did you manage to get here so quick? It’s astonishing, a dream!”

“Mr. Perhotin informed us that when you came to him, you held in your hands ... your blood-stained hands ... your money ... a lot of money ... a bundle of hundred-rouble notes, and that his servant-boy saw it too.”
“That’s true, gentlemen. I remember it was so.”

“Now, there’s one small point that arises. Can you tell us,” Nikolay Parfenovitch began, with extreme gentleness, “where did you get so much money all of a sudden, when it appears from the facts, from the reckoning of time, that you had not been home?”
The prosecutor’s brows contracted at the question being put so plainly, but he did not interrupt Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“No, I didn’t go home,” Mitya answered, apparently perfectly composed, but looking at the floor.

“Allow me then to repeat my question,” Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, as though creeping up on the subject. “Where were you able to come by such a sum all at once, when by your own admission, at five o’clock the same day, you —”

“I was short ten roubles and pawned my pistols with Perhotin, and then went to Madame Hohlakov to borrow three thousand, which she wouldn’t give me, and so on and so on, and all the rest of it,” Mitya interrupted sharply. “Yes, gentlemen, I was short of it, and then suddenly thousands turned up, eh? Do you know, gentlemen, you are both afraid now ‘what if he won’t tell us where he got it?’ That’s exactly how it is. I am not going to tell you, gentlemen. You’ve guessed right. You’ll never know,” said Mitya, chipping out each word with extraordinary determination. The lawyers were silent for a moment.
“You must understand, Mr. Karamazov, that it is of vital importance for us to know,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, softly and smoothly.
“I understand; but still, I won’t tell you.”

The prosecutor, too, intervened, and again reminded the prisoner that he was at liberty to refuse to answer questions, if he thought it in his interest, and so on. But in view of the damage he might do himself by his silence, especially in a case of such importance as —

“And so on, gentlemen, and so on. Enough! I’ve heard that rigmarole before,” Mitya interrupted again. “I can see for myself how important it is, and that this is the vital point, and still I won’t say.”
“What is it to us? It’s not our business, but yours. You are doing yourself harm,” observed Nikolay Parfenovitch nervously.

“You see, gentlemen, joking aside” — Mitya lifted his eyes and looked firmly at both of them — “I had a feeling from the first that we’d come to loggerheads at this point. But at first, when I began to give my evidence, it was all still far off and hazy; it was all vague, and I was so naive that I began on the assumption that mutual confidence existed between us. Now I can see for myself that such confidence is out of the question, since in any case we were bound to come to this cursed stumbling-block. And now we’ve come to it! It’s impossible, and that’s an end of it! But I don’t blame you. You can’t simply take my word for it all. I understand that, of course.”
He relapsed into gloomy silence.

“Couldn’t you, without abandoning your resolution to stay silent about the main point, could you not at the same time give us some slight hint as to the nature of the motives that are strong enough to make you refuse to answer, at a moment so full of danger to yourself?”
Mitya smiled mournfully, almost dreamily.

“I’m much more good-natured than you think, gentlemen. I’ll tell you the reason, and I’ll give you that hint, though you don’t deserve it. I won’t speak of it, gentlemen, because it would be a stain on my honor. The answer to the question of where I got the money would expose me to far greater disgrace than the murder and robbery of my father, if I had murdered and robbed him. That’s why I can’t tell you. I can’t, for fear of disgrace. What, gentlemen, are you going to write that down?”
“Yes, we’ll write it down,” lisped Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“You ought not to write that down about ‘disgrace.’ I only told you that out of the goodness of my heart. I didn’t have to tell you. I made you a present of it, so to speak, and you pounce on it at once. Oh, well — write, write what you like,” he concluded, with scornful disgust. “I’m not afraid of you, and I can still hold my head high in front of you.”
“And can’t you tell us the nature of that disgrace?” Nikolay Parfenovitch ventured.
The prosecutor frowned darkly.

“No, no, c’est fini, don’t trouble yourselves. It’s not worth soiling one’s hands. I’ve soiled myself enough because of you already. You’re not worth it — no one is ... Enough, gentlemen. I’m not going on.”
This was said too peremptorily. Nikolay Parfenovitch did not press further, but he could see from Ippolit Kirillovitch’s eyes that he had not given up hope.
“Can you not, at least, tell us what sum you had in your hands when you went into Mr. Perhotin’s — how many roubles exactly?”
“I can’t tell you that.”
“You mentioned to Mr. Perhotin, I believe, that you had received three thousand from Madame Hohlakov.”
“Perhaps I did. Enough, gentlemen. I won’t say how much I had.”
“Will you be so kind, then, as to tell us how you came here, and what you have done since you arrived?”
“Oh! you could ask the people here about that. But I’ll tell you if you like.”

He proceeded to do so, but we won’t repeat his story. He told it dryly and briefly. Of the raptures of his love, he said nothing, but told them that he had abandoned his determination to shoot himself, owing to “new factors in the case.” He told the story without going into motives or details. And this time the lawyers did not trouble him much. It was obvious that there was no essential point of interest to them here.

“We shall verify all that. We will come back to it during the examination of the witnesses, which will, of course, take place in your presence,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch in conclusion. “And now allow me to ask you to lay on the table everything in your possession, especially all the money you still have on you.”

“My money, gentlemen? Certainly. I understand that that is necessary. I’m actually surprised you haven’t asked about it sooner. It’s true I couldn’t get away anywhere. I’m sitting here where I can be seen. But here’s my money — count it, take it. That’s all, I think.”

He turned it all out of his pockets; even the small change — two twenty-kopeck pieces — he pulled out of his waistcoat pocket. They counted the money, which amounted to eight hundred and thirty-six roubles, and forty kopecks.
“And is that all?” asked the investigating lawyer.
“Yes.”
“You stated just now in your evidence that you spent three hundred roubles at Plotnikovs’. You gave Perhotin ten, your driver twenty, you lost two hundred here, then....”
Nikolay Parfenovitch reckoned it all up. Mitya helped him readily. They recalled every kopeck and included it in the reckoning. Nikolay Parfenovitch hurriedly added up the total.
“With this eight hundred you must have had around fifteen hundred at the start?”
“I suppose so,” Mitya snapped.
“How is it that everybody claims there was much more?”
“Let them claim it.”
“But you claimed it yourself.”
“Yes, I did, too.”

“We will compare all this with the evidence of other witnesses not yet examined. Don’t be anxious about your money. It will be properly taken care of, and will be at your disposal at the conclusion of ... what is beginning ... if it appears, or, so to speak, is proved, that you have undisputed right to it. Well, and now....”
Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly got up and informed Mitya firmly that it was his duty and obligation to conduct a thorough and detailed search “of your clothes and everything else....”
“By all means, gentlemen. I’ll turn out all my pockets, if you like.”
And he did, in fact, begin turning out his pockets.
“It will be necessary to take off your clothes, too.”
“What! Undress? Ugh! Damn it! Won’t you search me as I am? Can’t you?”
“It’s utterly impossible, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You must take off your clothes.”
“As you like,” Mitya submitted gloomily; “only, please, not here, but behind the curtains. Who’s going to search them?”
“Behind the curtains, of course.”
Nikolay Parfenovitch bent his head in assent. His small face wore an expression of peculiar solemnity.
